intro: Tuesday’s edition leads with a browser security update and two Canadian economic releases that reward a closer reading. Gasoline explains much of September’s inflation acceleration, while the timing of business interviews complicates an apparent improvement in confidence. Markets below use Tuesday’s reported closing session. For dinner planning, Vij’s has announced a closure next week.

stories.title: Firefox update closes a certificate-blocking gap
stories.summary: Mozilla’s October 20 security advisory identifies Firefox 158.0.1 as a high-impact update. One consequential change concerns compromised intermediate eMudhra certificates. Mozilla distributed a OneCRL block through RemoteSettings on October 17; the browser release now includes that updated block list itself. This extends the protection to installations where policy disables RemoteSettings or the network prevents its delivery. For people maintaining managed browsers, that distinction makes checking the installed version useful even when centrally distributed security settings normally arrive automatically. The advisory also lists incorrect SVG boundary conditions, uninitialized memory in the audio component and a PDF-viewer denial-of-service issue, with different severity ratings. Apply the appropriate Firefox update and check that it completed. The certificate fix addresses a specific distribution gap; the advisory does not establish that all the listed vulnerabilities have been exploited. Its practical message is straightforward: receiving an earlier remote block and installing the patched browser are separate mechanisms for delivering this protection.

stories.title: September’s price pressure is concentrated in fuel
stories.summary: Statistics Canada’s October 19 release puts annual inflation at 3.1% in September, up from 3.0% in August. Gasoline prices accelerated to 27.8% above a year earlier, compared with 22.8% in August. Excluding gasoline, inflation slowed to 2.2% from 2.4%. That split matters for household budgeting: the headline acceleration does not describe an equal increase in pressure across every spending category. Grocery inflation slowed to 1.7% from 2.8%, although grocery prices remained 33.0% above September 2020. Fresh vegetables were cheaper than a year earlier, while beef continued to show a substantial annual increase. Overall consumer prices rose 0.1% during September, or 0.4% after seasonal adjustment. Those monthly measures answer a different question from the annual headline and should not be interchanged. The report offers a more specific picture than a general claim that everything is accelerating: fuel pressure strengthened while several other categories moderated. Slower inflation still means prices are rising, unless a category’s measured change is negative.

stories.title: Business optimism improved before renewed trade friction
stories.summary: The Bank of Canada’s October 19 Business Outlook Survey reports improved third-quarter sentiment and sales expectations. Its timing is essential: interviews ran August 6–September 2, and about three-quarters preceded the breakdown in Canada–US trade talks and new Canadian counter-tariffs. Subsequent responses point to weaker export and investment outlooks, alongside renewed pressure on costs and inflation expectations. Hiring intentions remained soft, with most firms planning unchanged staffing. Investment intentions eased slightly but remained robust, supported at some businesses by demand and commodity prices. For readers monitoring recession risk, this combination warrants more care than either an all-clear or an imminent-downturn claim. The survey captures business expectations at particular moments, and later developments can change their meaning. Its earlier improvement and later deterioration should be read together. Neither the headline sentiment reading nor the recession-planning share below establishes whether Canada is currently in recession.

dining.title: Vij’s announces a Tuesday closure
dining.description: Vij’s official website lists October 27 as a closure for a private event, with regular hours resuming the following day. Account for that interruption before arranging dinner at the Cambie Street restaurant next week. The website lists normal opening time as 5:30 p.m. daily, but the dated closure takes precedence for that Tuesday. This is a verified availability change rather than a public event or a new-menu announcement.
